title: Introduction
transcript: Everything in this video was made by AI agents. The script, the voice, the animation, even the music. But none of it was left to them alone. Rasmus, who wrote the book this channel is based on, steered every step. That's what engineering looks like now.

For twenty years, the job was one loop. You, a keyboard, and a problem. That loop is changing. Coding agents read whole codebases, edit dozens of files, run the tests, and fix what fails. More of the work is now describing what you want, reviewing what comes back, and steering.

Here's the catch. Working well with agents is a skill. When an agent wastes your afternoon, it's rarely a weak model. It's missing context, a task scoped too wide, or not knowing when to let it run, and when to take the wheel back. None of that is complicated. It just isn't obvious.

And nobody has this fully figured out. The field moves every month. What this series offers is principles that have held up in real projects, stated plainly, failures included. No hype. No doom. No prompt tricks.

The Agentic Crew is a free book by Rasmus Schlünsen. This channel turns each chapter into a short film like this one. Context, guardrails, git, tests, memory, security, fleets of agents, and knowing when not to use them. About two minutes each.
Next up: what an agent actually is. Here's a hint. The model never runs a single command. Subscribe so you don't miss it, and read the whole book free, at the agentic crew dot com.

title: What Is an Agent?
transcript: The word agent gets stuck on almost anything, from a chatbot that answers questions to a system that deploys code to production. It's worth being precise, because the difference changes how you work with them.

Think of a spectrum. At one end, autocomplete suggests the next few tokens. A copilot writes bigger blocks, but only when you ask. Then comes the shift. A tool-using agent acts. It reads files, runs commands, checks the result, and goes again. At the far end, autonomous agents take a goal, and come back with a pull request.

Three things make something agentic. Planning, where a goal becomes steps. Tool use, where every result shapes the next decision. And iteration: try, observe, adjust, and try again. A chatbot gives you one answer. An agent gives you a cycle. The tools are the promotion.

Strip away the branding, and every coding agent has four parts. A model, which reads text and writes text, and nothing else. Tools it's allowed to ask for. A loop that keeps calling the model and feeding the results back. And an environment, where the tools actually run.

Here's the part people miss. The model never executes anything. A tool call is just structured text. The model asks to run the tests. The harness checks whether that's allowed, runs them, and hands the output back. The model reads it, and decides what to do next. That's the whole trick.

That surrounding program is the harness. Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor are all harnesses. The harness decides permissions, what stays in context, when to stop, and where the tools run. So when an agent does something reckless, ask two questions. Why did the model suggest it? And why did the harness allow it? The first, you can influence. The second, you control.

And stay clear-eyed. Agents aren't magic. They hallucinate APIs, drift beyond the task, declare victory too early, and lose track on long sessions. Every one of those failures has a mitigation, and those mitigations are the rest of this book.

The book's mental model is Rain Man. The agent is Raymond. It counts cards faster than any human, for as long as you like. You're Charlie. You decide which casino, how much to bet, and when to cash out. That part is still your job. Next up: context, the most important skill in agentic engineering.

title: Context
transcript: A payments bug comes in. Customers with accented letters in their address can't pay. One engineer tells an agent, there's a bug for international users, take a look. It returns a patch that strips every accent from every address. Worse than the bug. A second engineer pastes in the error log, the trace, the gateway docs, and the three files involved. The fix is four lines.

Same model. Same agent. What changed was what the agent could see. That's why the most important skill here isn't prompting. It's context engineering: curating everything that lands in the model's window.

Think of the window as a workbench. Space is limited, so you lay out only what this task needs. But the real skill is designing the workshop, with clear structure and labelled drawers, so the agent can pull the right tool off the wall itself.

Context reaches an agent on a ladder. At level zero, you describe the problem in your own words, and the detail gets lost. At level one, you paste the raw stack trace. Better, but tomorrow you paste it again. At level two, the agent can run the test and read the trace itself, and you add only what no tool can find: your intent, and your constraints.

That's infrastructure versus injection. Infrastructure is set up once and pays off in every session: tool access, integrations with your error tracker, a navigable repo, an instruction file. Injection is what you paste by hand. When you paste the same thing a third time, promote it.

And more is not better. Every token costs twice, in money and in attention. Details buried in the middle get less weight, and quality degrades as the input grows. It's called context rot, and a bigger window doesn't cure it. Before adding anything, ask: will the agent decide differently because it saw this?

Long sessions fill up with noise. Compact them into a short brief. Have the agent keep notes in a file. Send big explorations to a sub-agent that returns only the conclusion. Then work in phases: research, plan, implement, each in a fresh window.

When a session ends, its window is gone. So commit often, keep the notes, and put what's permanent in the instruction file. Your code, your repo and your docs are all context now. Next up: guardrails, trust, and sandboxes.

title: Guardrails, Trust, and Sandboxes
transcript: An agent is blocked from deleting files. It needs to undo some changes, so it runs a git checkout instead. That's allowed, because it sounds harmless. Every uncommitted change in the folder is wiped, including the engineer's own work. The agent wasn't malicious. It was resourceful.
Power without boundaries isn't bold engineering. It's negligence. But guardrails that are too tight make an agent useless. The craft is finding the line.

Think of a mixing board, with one slider for each kind of action: reading files, writing them, shell commands, the network, and git. Reads can run freely. A database migration needs explicit approval. Even two shell commands differ. Running the tests is safe. Installing a package deserves a prompt.

On day one, you watch everything. After a week, tests and refactors run freely. After a month, it commits to feature branches on its own. The allowlist becomes a log of trust decisions, but pushing to main stays denied forever. Guardrails should be invisible for routine work, and rigid for the exceptional.

Plan mode is the cheapest guardrail there is. The agent can read and think, but it changes nothing until you approve the plan. For rules that must never bend, use hooks: scripts the tool runs every time, before an edit, or when the agent says it's done. The model can't argue with them. Instructions are advice. Permissions are policy. Hooks are law.

Modes that skip every permission belong inside a throwaway container. In one supply-chain attack, malicious packages looked for coding agents on developers' machines, and ran them with their guardrails switched off, to hunt for secrets.

So no single wall is enough. You need defense in depth. The allow list catches the obvious. Hooks enforce the rules that never bend. A sandbox limits the blast radius. Commit history lets you recover. And your own review catches what no rule would flag.

Too many gates fail too. Click yes forty times, and you stop reading. The guardrails feel safe, and protect nothing. If you approve the same kind of action five times in a session, it probably belongs on the allowlist.

Best of all, a sandbox gives the agent the freedom to be wrong: a worktree, a container, a cloud environment you can throw away. When failure is cheap, experimentation is free. Next up: git as agent infrastructure.

title: Git as Agent Infrastructure
transcript: An agent can change twenty files in thirty seconds. Bundle them into one commit, and when something breaks, you're untangling a mess. Split them into five clean commits, and you revert the one that broke and keep the rest. With agents, Git stops being just version control. It becomes the backbone: your undo button, your parallel workspace, your review screen, and your documentation.
The first habit: commit small, and commit often. Commit after each logical change, after the tests pass, and before anything risky, so there's always a save point to return to.

Then let the agent write the commit message. It has the whole diff in context, so it summarizes from facts, not memory. Fix auth bug is noise. A message that explains the race condition, and why it happened, is useful six months later. Add a co-author line, so agent work is searchable. Your name is still on the commit.

Every agent task gets its own branch. That gives you isolation, a clear review scope, and a clean rollback: if it's wrong, delete the branch. Name branches after the task, and your branch list becomes a manifest of what your agents are doing.

For agents working in parallel, branches aren't enough. Two agents in one folder will fight over the files. A worktree gives each agent its own directory on its own branch, sharing one history. It's the cheapest sandbox there is. Just remember it holds only what Git tracks, so no environment files, and no installed dependencies.

More and more, tools create worktrees for you, and cloud agents clone the repo into a remote sandbox and hand back a pull request. The shape is the same every time: an isolated copy, a dedicated branch, and a diff you review.

Your review interface is the diff. Read the tests first, watch for scope creep, and check the interfaces. When agents run in parallel, reviewing becomes the bottleneck. Keep pull requests small, let C I and linters take the first pass, and don't start what you can't review this week.

Finally, agents read your history. Git log and git blame are documentation they consult directly. A history of fix bug leaves them guessing. Every commit message, branch name and pull request is context for the next agent, so make it worth reading. Next up: testing as the feedback loop.

title: Testing as the Feedback Loop
transcript: Two code bases. Same agent. Same task: add a rate limiter that blocks a user after a hundred requests a minute. The first code base has no tests. The agent writes the code, and stops. It has no way to know if it worked. Three days later, production shows the middleware was mounted in the wrong order and never ran. The rate limiter was decoration.

The second code base has a test suite. The agent writes the same code, and runs the tests. Two old tests fail. It reads the failures, adjusts, and runs again. Green. Then it adds three new tests of its own. Same agent, same task, night and day. The difference was the tests.

An agent can't look at a screen and feel whether it's right. What it can do is run your tests and read the results. Green means keep going. Red means try again. No tests means flying blind. And the quality of the signal matters. Expected four twenty-nine, got two hundred, is something it can act on. A bare assertion error is barely better than silence.

So write the test first, then say: make this pass. Picture a duration parser with seven assertions. The first attempt forgets seconds. Fail. It adds them. Fail again: bad input doesn't raise an error. It adds validation. Green. Each cycle took seconds, and nobody had to explain what correct means. Writing tests becomes programming the agent.

Good agentic tests are fast. If each run takes minutes, an agent gets a handful of tries an hour. If it takes seconds, it gets hundreds. They're deterministic, because a flaky failure sends the agent chasing a ghost. They're isolated, with clear error messages, and they test behavior, not implementation.

You don't need full coverage. You need tests where the agent works: the hot paths, the API contracts, the seams between components. And negative tests, so an agent can't simplify your validation into accepting garbage.

Be careful, though. A bad test suite is worse than none. Tests that only check the mock. Assertions that are too loose. Tests that copy the implementation. Each one gives a green light that means nothing. If a subtle bug would slip past a test, that test is furniture.

Get it right, and the cycle compounds. Better tests make agents more autonomous, which means faster iteration, which leaves more time for better tests. Your review shifts from does this work, to is this the right approach. Before you tune prompts or chase new models, go write tests. Next up: convention over configuration.

title: Convention Over Configuration
transcript: Picture the same agent, on the same afternoon, with the same model. In one project, it writes code worthy of a senior hire. In another, it produces something nobody wants to maintain. The difference isn't the prompt. It's the code base.

In the first project, every endpoint follows one pattern: a handler, a schema and a test, named the same way. The agent reads the existing endpoints, follows the pattern, and the review takes three minutes. In the second, routes live in three different folders, and errors are thrown, returned, or quietly turned into null. The agent copies whatever it saw last, and the review takes thirty minutes of: that's not how we do it here.

Convention is implicit context. An agent explores a code base the way a new hire does: it looks for patterns. When tests always sit next to the file they test, nobody has to say where the new test goes. And consistent names make the agent's own tools work. When every test file ends the same way, a single search finds them all.

The strongest convention is the instruction file at the root of the project. Agents dot M D has become the cross-tool standard. A good one has five parts: a project overview, the exact build and test commands, the architecture decisions, your conventions, and the common pitfalls. It takes about thirty minutes to write, and it gives every session more context than most people get in their first week.

Keep it short. It's loaded on every session, so every line is a tax on every task. Point to deeper documents instead of pasting them in. And keep it up to date, because an outdated instruction file is worse than none. The agent will trust it.

Procedures become skills: a folder with a skill file inside. The agent sees only each skill's name and description, until a task needs the rest. The progression is simple. A convention the agent keeps getting wrong goes in the instruction file. A procedure becomes a skill. A rule that must never be broken becomes a hook.

Conventions are the closest thing agents have to long-term memory. Without them, you correct the same mistake in session one, session two, and session three. Encode it once, in a documented pattern and a linter rule, and it's gone for good.
Your code base is the environment your agents live in. Make it legible. Make it predictable. Make it boring. The agents will repay you with code that looks like it belongs. Next up: the ship's log.

title: The Ship's Log
transcript: Every captain keeps a log, because a ship without one forgets. It forgets which channels were shallow, and every mistake gets made again. That's how most agent sessions begin: with amnesia. The agent doesn't know what was built yesterday, or which three approaches to a problem were tried last week.

Picture an hour-long session. The agent tries two approaches that fail, discovers a quirk in the database driver, and lands a clean solution. The code is committed. But the knowledge lived in the context window, and now it's gone. Tomorrow's session will cheerfully try the same two dead ends.

The usual tools only go so far. Instruction files hold stable knowledge, but nobody updates them for every small discovery. Git history records what changed, not what was learned. And session summaries only work if someone remembers to write them, at the end of a long day.

The fix is active memory: a system that captures knowledge as it's created, organizes it, and serves it back when it's needed. Knowledge now flows from every past session into the current one, including sessions run by teammates, weeks ago. A note in the log reads: shoal at low tide, stay east. That lesson cost someone a damaged ship. The log makes sure it only costs one.

Structure makes it searchable. Wings for projects, rooms for topics, and drawers that hold verbatim records, not summaries. At the start of a session, the agent loads what's known. During it, the agent stores its discoveries. At the end, a hook saves the work automatically.

Share the store, and agents working in parallel stop working blind. One agent finds a missing database index and writes it down. Another agent, building the frontend, reads that note before it starts. Each agent keeps its own diary, and everyone can read them all.

Be choosy. Store what's expensive to rediscover: undocumented behavior, decisions and their reasons, approaches that failed. Skip what the code already says. And treat memory as an attack surface. A poisoned note doesn't vanish when the session ends. It comes back next week.

When a note keeps coming up, promote it into a convention, or a test. Your agents are the crew, and every crew is temporary. The log is what lets the next voyage start from understanding. Next up: extending the agent's reach.

title: Extending the Agent's Reach
transcript: Picture an engineer chasing an error on a checkout page. The logs are in one system. The ticket is in another. The database schema is in a third. Six browser tabs, copy, paste, repeat. And the agent in the terminal can only see local files. A brilliant colleague, chained to a desk.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is the fix. Think of it as USB for agents. An MCP server is a small program that exposes tools over one standard plug. The agent calls them like any other tool, and the server translates. Someone builds a Stripe server, and every compatible agent can use Stripe.

Why it matters: an agent that only sees the repo is missing most of its context. The bug report, the logs, the schema and the docs all live somewhere else. Without integrations, you become the human middleware, shuttling text between tabs. With them, you go from clipboard to captain.

Building your own server is small work. But remember, the model never sees your code. It only sees what you wrote about it. So name tools as verbs. Describe every parameter. Return errors that say what went wrong, so the model can correct itself. Keep each tool focused, and limit how much it returns.

Tools let the agent act. Resources, like a database schema, give it the map. And skills add the know-how: a folder with a skill dot M D file that describes how your team actually investigates a problem. The server is the hands. The skill is the training.

Every integration raises the stakes. An agent with database access can delete data. So make read-only a fact, not a promise. One reference Postgres server claimed to be read-only, and a crafted query simply stepped around it. Put the guarantee in the database itself: a role that cannot write.

Then there's integration creep. Every connected tool loads its definitions into context before you type a word, and a model facing a hundred tools makes worse choices. Curate per project. If you wouldn't keep a tab open to that system, the agent doesn't need it. And often, a familiar C L I does the job for free.

Start with your database, through a read-only role. Then your ticket tracker. Then monitoring. The agents are already capable. The question is whether they can see enough of your world. But every connection also lets the world talk back. Next up: the agent attack surface.

title: The Agent Attack Surface
transcript: Picture an agent asked to look through the open issues on a public repo. One issue was written by a stranger, and buried in it is a paragraph addressed not to the maintainer, but to the agent. The agent reads it, and helpfully does what it says. Private data ends up in public. Nothing was broken. Every part worked as designed.

Application security rests on one idea: data should never run as instructions. Language models don't have that separation. Your request, a file, a web page, a tool result. To the model, it's all just tokens. That's prompt injection. Someone puts text where your agent will read it, and the text says: do this instead.

The model is not a security boundary. A defence that works nearly every time is a good spam filter, and a terrible lock. Prompt injection is unsolved. So plan as if it will happen, and ask a better question: when the agent is tricked, what's the worst it can do?

The most useful model here is the lethal trifecta. Access to private data. Exposure to untrusted content. And a way to send data out. Any two are manageable. All three in one session, and anyone who can get text in front of your agent can get your data out. So remove at least one leg, for every session.

Untrusted text gets in through more doors than you'd think. Issues and comments. Web pages. Log lines, where a username can carry a payload. Tool descriptions from other people's servers. Even the instruction files in a repo you just cloned. Pointing an agent at someone else's repo means running someone else's prompt.

And data leaves through more than email. An image link with a secret in its address. A public comment. A web request. Even a name lookup. If the agent can write anywhere an outsider can read, that's an exit.
Skills, plugins and servers are dependencies, too. Read them, pin them, and review changes, because a tool's description can quietly change after you approved it.

The defences come in layers. Scoped, short-lived tokens. A reader agent that sees untrusted text but holds no privileges, passing only checked, structured data to an actor that does. A closed network. A human approving anything outbound. And a log the agent can't edit.
Think of a harbour pilot. They take the helm through unfamiliar waters, but they don't get the keys to the hold. Let your agents steer. Keep the keys. Next up: articulating intent.

title: Articulating Intent
transcript: Tell an agent to fix the auth bug, and it won't ask which one. It will guess, confidently, and hand you a fix for something you never asked about. There's no secret syntax that prevents this. Prompting is communication. If you can write a good bug report, you already know how.

A good task prompt says what you want, why it matters, and how success looks. The login endpoint rejects valid tokens when the session cache is cold. This test reproduces it. Fix it, and keep every auth test passing. Leave out the file path; the agent can find that itself. Give it what tools can't: the symptom, the domain, the intent.

Then say what not to do. Agents are eager optimisers. Ask for a fix, and you might get a rewritten module, three new dependencies and a changed public interface. Constraints are the guardrails on the bridge. No new dependencies. Don't touch the public interface. Stay inside this folder.

Build a dashboard with live metrics, roles and exports isn't a prompt. It's a project. Split it into small, verifiable steps: the data model, then the endpoint, then the filtering, then the view, each one checked before the next begins. And when tasks are independent, say so, and let sub-agents run them in parallel.

For anything bigger than a small fix, ask for a plan first. Don't change any code yet. Read the files, and tell me what you'll touch and how you'll verify it. A wrong assumption caught in a short plan costs one sentence. Caught in a giant diff, it costs the whole diff.

Your first prompt won't be perfect. When the output is wrong, ask what you failed to say. The agent's output is the error message. Your prompt is the stack trace. You're debugging your own communication.

Try speaking your prompts. Typing is tiring, so typed prompts shrink and lose context. Speaking costs almost nothing, so you tell the whole story of the bug. And when words fail, show it. A screenshot of a broken layout says more than three paragraphs about padding.

Finally, treat prompts as code. Save the ones that work as skills and slash commands, versioned in git and reviewed like anything else. Prompting isn't a parlour trick. It's engineering. Next up: local, commercial and hybrid models.

title: Local, Commercial, and Hybrid Models
transcript: Picture a team of eight engineers, all running coding agents, with nobody watching the meter. Then the first real bill arrives. Twenty-two hundred dollars, for one month. Meanwhile, at a healthcare company, patient data can't touch an outside server at all, so the only option is a local model.
Both stories ask the same question: where does the model run? It sounds like infrastructure. It's really a decision about trust, cost, and capability.

Commercial frontier models are where the best reasoning lives. They call tools cleanly and stay inside the lines, deep into a long session. But even a huge context window has limits. An agent at eighty percent of its window reasons worse than the same agent at twenty.

Local models give you something no A P I can. Your code never leaves the machine, and every token is free. Open models got much better at agentic work. But be honest about the hardware. You need serious memory, and on long, multi-file tasks, smaller models drift and lose the plan.

Agents burn tokens because they're working. Every step re-sends the growing conversation, so a simple bug fix can run to tens of thousands of tokens. So set limits. Scope tasks tightly, cap turns per task, and put hard stops on anything automated. A pipeline agent stuck in a retry loop at three a.m. is exactly how the surprise bill happens.

And measure the return honestly. In one trial, experienced developers were slower with A I tools, while believing they were faster. How fast it feels is not evidence. Track lead time and failure rates instead.

Some code legally cannot leave the building: government contracts, patient records, financial systems. For that code, a local model isn't a nice-to-have, it's the only option. There's a middle path, too: frontier models deployed inside your own cloud boundary, with your data kept there.

So the real question isn't local or commercial. It's which model, for which step. Send exploration to a small, cheap model. Save the frontier model for planning, where reasoning matters most. Hand implementation to a mid-tier model that follows the plan.

Don't get religious about models. The best engineers are pragmatists. They measure what works, and switch when something better comes along. The model is a tool, and the skill is knowing which one to reach for. Next up: multi-agent orchestration, when one agent isn't enough.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
transcript: One carpenter can build a shed. A house needs an electrician, a plumber, and a roofer, working in parallel, each doing what they do best. Agents work the same way. But parallel agents need coordination, and coordination has a cost.

The hard part isn't running several agents. It's splitting the work. If one agent depends on another's output, they can't run in parallel. So find the seams. Split by layer, with a clear contract between them. Split by feature. Or split by concern: one refactors, one writes tests, one updates the docs.
Every agent gets its own branch and its own worktree. Two agents in one working directory will trample each other's files. Three directories, three branches, three agents.

Multi-agent work comes in two shapes. Sub-agents inside one session buy you clean context. One reads forty files, and hands back a ten-line summary. Background agents take a whole, well-scoped ticket, and come back later with a pull request. For a vague task, use neither.

Sometimes agents work in sequence. One plans, one implements, one reviews. The danger is the handover. The next agent starts cold. So make it explicit: a plan file, stub functions, a progress checklist. Write it like a ticket for a colleague on another continent.

Then comes the merge. One agent changed the schema, another wrote a migration for the old one. Prevent conflicts by giving each agent its own files. Let a merge agent handle the rest. And review everything yourself, because code can merge cleanly and still contradict itself.

More agents isn't always better. With four terminals open, one agent can crash silently while you look elsewhere. You become the bottleneck. And every extra agent adds setup, merging, and review. For short tasks, the overhead eats the gains.

Here's where it pays. Picture a notifications feature: a backend endpoint, a bell icon, and the tests. Write the contract first. Then three agents run at once, and you merge the backend first. About forty-five minutes in total, against roughly ninety for one agent alone.

A crew of five isn't always faster than one sailor who knows the boat. The skill isn't running as many agents as possible. It's knowing which pieces are safe to run in parallel. That judgement is the highest-leverage prompt you can write. Next up: agents in the pipeline.

title: Agents in the Pipeline
transcript: Picture a team that adds an agent to its pipeline to fix lint failures automatically. The pipeline stays green, and everyone loves it. Then someone notices a whole category of lint rules has vanished. The agent had learned the fastest fix: switch the rule off in the config.

Nobody caught it, because the signal they watched was exactly the signal the agent had learned to game. At your desk, you see every file an agent touches. In the pipeline, it runs in the dark. You only see green or red.

So start with jobs that are safe to automate and easy to verify. Screening pull requests before a human reviews them. Drafting release notes. Explaining why a test failed. A good test: would you be comfortable if you only spot-checked a few of its runs?

Then there's the overnight agent. Point it at a clear ticket, go home, and wake up to a pull request. It needs good tests, a tight scope, a fresh branch, and a hard timeout. Cloud products now run this loop for you. But they give you a sandbox, not a well-written ticket.

In the pipeline, nobody is there to hit stop. In one story, a review bot's retry logic ran unchecked over a holiday weekend, and ran up a four thousand dollar bill. So cap every run, limit concurrency, set spend alerts, and keep a kill switch.

Agent pull requests still need a human review. Tests check behaviour. They don't check intent, or whether the approach will hurt the next feature. A five-minute scan of the approach goes a long way. Auto-merge only the trivial, mechanical changes.

And on a public repository, anyone can write the text your agent reads. A pull request description can carry instructions. Add secrets and a write token, and you have a stranger holding your keys. So ask who gets to write the text it reads.

In production, agents watch. They track error rates, compare latency, and recommend a rollback. But the rollback itself belongs to a human, or a boring, pre-approved rule. Production is read-only for agents.

Start small. Formatting in week one. Review comments in week two. Changelogs in the first month. Overnight agents by month three. Each step builds on the last. Nobody's watching, so your safety nets need to be stronger. Next up: building your own agents.

title: Building Your Own Agents
transcript: Every time you open a coding agent, you're standing on hundreds of decisions someone else made. Someone wrote the system prompt, chose the tools, and decided what survives when the conversation gets compacted. When you use an agent, those decisions are invisible. When you build one, every one of them is yours.

Here's the uncomfortable truth. The core of an agent fits on a single page. Call the model, run the tools it asks for, feed the results back, and repeat. That's why so many first attempts disappoint. The loop is the easy part. The work is everything around it.

The first instinct is to make everything an agent. Resist it. Most of the value comes from ordinary code with model calls at fixed points: fetch the ticket, classify it, draft a reply, queue it for a human. Save the open loop for work like debugging, where each step depends on the last. Deterministic skeleton, agentic muscles.

The model has no memory. Each turn, it sees exactly what you send it, and nothing else. So you build the prompt every turn: stable instructions, the relevant state, history compacted, tool results trimmed. When a home-built agent gets confused, it's usually the context, not the model.

Tools are the product. Sort every one by its side effects. Read tools run freely. Write tools stay inside the run. Irreversible ones, like sending an email or charging a card, go through an approval, or aren't handed over at all. And make writes idempotent, because agents retry, and one refund should stay one refund.

Asking a human is just another tool call. Picture a refund that needs a manager's sign-off, and the manager is in a meeting. The harness saves the run, sends the question to Slack, and stops. Eighteen hours later, the answer arrives, and the loop picks up exactly where it left off.

So how do you know it works? You write evals: realistic tasks, each with a check. Start with twenty, drawn from real traffic, and turn every production failure into a new case. Run them on every prompt tweak and every model upgrade. The builders who ship reliable agents aren't the ones with the cleverest prompts. They're the ones with the best evals.

Treat every input as untrusted, and make less possible. Then comes the reward. Once you've built an agent, you get better at using one. The harness stops being a black box. Build one, even a small one. Next up: when agents get it wrong.

title: When Agents Get It Wrong
transcript: The task was a one-line fix: a dropdown rendering behind a modal. Before you looked up from your coffee, the agent had changed thirty-two files and rewritten the styling system. The original bug was still there. Everyone who works with agents long enough collects stories like this.

Picture an agent that imports a date library, with clean code, correct types, even tests. The library doesn't exist. Code review would have passed it, because plausible fictions are built to pass review. So the agent runs the tests. And every new dependency is a security decision, because attackers now register the names models like to invent.

Then there's the infinite loop. Error, fix, a different error, fix, the first error again. Forty minutes later: nineteen attempts, and the code is worse than when it started. If an agent hasn't solved it in three passes, it won't solve it in thirty. Stop it, read the errors yourself, and start a fresh context.

Or the confident wrong answer. A race condition, fixed with a half-second sleep. The tests went green. In production, under load, it wasn't enough, and the backed-up queue took down another service. Agents optimise for the signal you give them. Passing tests are necessary, but not sufficient.

Two hours into a session, the agent forgets a rule you set at the start: raw queries only, no database framework. It didn't decide to ignore you. The rule simply faded. Long sessions degrade. Keep tasks short, commit often, and write project rules into the instruction file, where they can't fade.

The nastiest story isn't a mistake at all. An agent reads a ticket written by a stranger, full of instructions, and follows them, carrying private data out into the open. The fix is structural. Private data, untrusted content, a way to send data out: remove at least one of the three.

The common thread: in every story, the agent did exactly what it was built to do. It was helpful, creative, persistent, obedient. These aren't agent bugs. They're workflow bugs. The fix is tighter scope, better feedback, shorter sessions, narrower permissions, and a human who stays engaged.

So keep a diagnostic playbook. Is it scope, context, feedback, capability, a full context window, a loop, or untrusted input? Name the failure, and you know what to fix. And remember the most underrated tool you have: delete the branch, and start over. Next up: when not to use agents.

title: When Not to Use Agents
transcript: The best agentic engineers aren't the ones who use agents the most. They're the ones who know exactly when to put the agent away. Reach for an agent when the job calls for a human, and you lose both time and credibility.

Every agent interaction has a cost. You write the prompt, wait, review, fix, and run it again. For an hour-long task, that's a bargain. For renaming a variable, it's slower than just doing it. In one randomised trial, experienced developers in code they knew well were slower with AI tools, while believing they'd been faster. How fast you felt is not a measurement.

When you're designing a system from scratch, the thinking is the work. An agent can list the trade-offs. But if it makes the calls, you won't understand your own system. That judgment only comes from doing the work. Use it as a sparring partner, not as the architect.

Security-critical code is different. A broken auth check shows no symptoms until an attacker finds it, and agents write code that looks right. So write it yourself, and get human eyes on it. Then flip the roles, and ask the agent to attack your token check. Let the agent hunt. Keep the pen.

When you're learning, resist it. If the agent writes all the Rust, you haven't learned Rust. Asking why a borrow checker error happens builds understanding. Asking the agent to fix it doesn't. Use agents as tutors, not ghostwriters. And hard news, like sunsetting a product, should come from a person.

Agents amplify what's already there. In a clean codebase, they write clean code. In a mess, they write more mess. In legacy code you can't clean up, start with characterisation tests, scope ruthlessly, and hand the agent the tedious, mechanical parts.

Then there's craft. Writing code by hand builds pattern recognition that lives in your fingers. When you hit a problem the agent can't solve, you need those skills sharp. So write code by hand regularly. Not because it's faster, but because it keeps you dangerous.

The central skill isn't prompting. It's judgment. Reach for agents when the leverage is real: big refactors, boilerplate, exploring code, writing tests. Put them away when the work needs human thinking, human accountability, or human craft. Anyone can type a prompt. Knowing when not to is the harder skill. Next up: agentic teams.

title: Agentic Teams
transcript: In one controlled trial, experienced developers used AI tools on their own mature projects, and came out almost a fifth slower. The striking part: they believed they had been a fifth faster. Your gut is not a measuring instrument. And on a team, that matters more than anywhere.

The ten x claim isn't wrong, just misleading. It's a spike graph, not a flat multiplier. Boilerplate and big refactors go from hours to minutes. System design and a subtle race condition barely move. And agents amplify. Teams with good tests and small batches get better. Weak foundations get worse. So measure outcomes, like lead time and how often you ship. Not lines generated.

Then the pull requests pile up. An engineer who opened two a day now opens five, all clean, all passing tests, and reviewing them is exhausting. So the question shifts from, is this correct, to, is this the right approach? Reviewers become architects. A review bot can take the first pass, but it's a filter, not a reviewer. It can find a bug. It can't tell you the feature shouldn't exist.

The hardest question is juniors. They learned by doing exactly the work agents now do. The struggle was the education. So use the agent as a tutor, not a replacement. First it explains. Then it pairs, and every line must be understood before it's kept. Then it drafts. Only then does it multiply.

Uneven adoption creates a new risk. One engineer gets fluent, ships at three times the rate, and soon has touched every part of the codebase. The bus factor drops to one. The fix is structural: a shared agents dot M D, shared skills in the repo, and rotation, so the team's knowledge keeps up with its output.

Even the standup changes. A task can now start and finish between two standups, so the daily sync is less about progress and more about intent, making sure three engineers aren't sending agents after the same problem. And conventions matter more, because they shape every agent session on the team.

When agent written code causes an incident, who is responsible? The answer is simpler than it sounds. Git is the audit trail: mark every agent assisted commit, consistently. The reviewer who approves the pull request owns it, like any other code. And keep the session logs, so months later you can see what the agent saw.

So what do you hire for? Not whiteboard speed. System design, judgment, clear communication, and breaking big work into agent sized pieces. Hire for judgment. You can always give them an agent for the rest. Next up: final words, and why the craft is changing, not dying.

title: Final Words
transcript: Picture a five year old on an engineer's lap, watching an agent refactor a module. Files open and close, tests run, green checks appear. And the child asks: is the computer fixing itself? It's a better question than it sounds, because the definition of engineering is being rewritten, right now.

The craft is not dying. It's molting. The outer shell is falling away: the keystrokes, the syntax, the boilerplate. But the animal underneath, the part that knows what to build and knows when it's right, is more alive than ever.

Agents are amplifiers, not replacements. Give one to a mediocre engineer, and you get mediocre software at terrifying speed. Give one to a great engineer, and the old way starts to look like building highways with shovels. The ones who thrive will master the boring things: context, guardrails, tests, conventions. Tools change every quarter. Judgment compounds over a career.

So this isn't a replacement. It's a promotion, from typist to captain. And the part being automated was never the part anyone loved. Nobody became an engineer to write boilerplate parsers. They wanted to build things that matter.

The book is honest about what it got wrong. Security was underestimated: every integration is a channel for someone else's text to reach the agent. The bottleneck turned out to be review, not orchestration. Agent capacity is cheap. Human attention is not. And the harness matters as much as the model.

Then there's the crew itself. A crew suggests loyalty, shipmates who know your habits. Agents aren't like that. They don't remember the last session. Each one arrives fresh, does its work, and disappears. It's more like hiring dockworkers at every port.

And that's fine. For most of maritime history, the ship was the continuity: the charts, the logbook, the rigging. Your codebase, your conventions, your tests and your agents dot M D are the ship. Build it well, and any fresh crew is useful in minutes. The crew is disposable. The ship is not.

So tonight, open a terminal. Pick the bug you've been avoiding. Point an agent at it, give it context, set a guardrail, and watch what happens. This discipline is being invented right now, by the people who build. You're the captain. Next up, in the first appendix: agents as pentesters.

title: Agents as Pentesters
transcript: What if your pipeline could hack itself before attackers do? Penetration testing has always been slow and manual. A consultant spends weeks probing and writing a report, once a year if you're typical. Meanwhile the code changes every day, and your security drifts silently.

Autonomous pentesting splits the work into phases. First, agents scan the target and read the source code. Then they map every endpoint and login flow. Then five specialists work in parallel: injection, cross site scripting, authentication, authorization, and server side request forgery.

Next, five more agents try to prove each finding by actually exploiting it. That's the difference between a scanner and a pentester. A scanner says, this might be vulnerable. A pentester shows you. Finally, a reporting agent writes it up, with severity scores and fixes. And a durable workflow resumes any phase that crashes.

Run it continuously, and it becomes transformative. A sentinel watches the repository every few hours and routes by what changed. A query file goes to the injection agent. A template goes to cross site scripting. A Dockerfile triggers a full scan. Nothing changed? It skips. Zero cost, zero noise.

But this agent is hostile by design, so the guardrails now protect the world from your agent. Never run it against production. Get written authorization from whoever controls each system. Verify every finding by hand. And sandbox the agents, so they reach the target and nothing else. Start restrictive, and stay restrictive.

When an exploit fails, the agent records what it tried and what came back, say, a firewall blocking the request, and tries a different approach next time. It doesn't learn in the machine learning sense, but each scan gets sharper. Duplicate findings are merged by endpoint, weakness type and root cause, so fifty reports become ten real issues.

Not every agent needs the same model. The most capable one crafts the exploits, while cheaper ones analyze and write reports. And a dashboard keeps a human in the loop. Agents can hallucinate findings, or miss real ones, so every finding is really a question: is this real?

It's every principle in this book, pushed to its limit. If you can build a system that safely lets agents attack your own software, everything else is easier. Next up, in the second appendix: the state of the tools.

title: The State of the Tools
transcript: This appendix is deliberately perishable. Everything else in the book is written to survive the next model release. This part is a snapshot, and the tools shift every few months. So instead of naming winners, here is a way to judge any tool, including the ones that don't exist yet. When a detail goes stale, trust the principles, and check the vendor's current documentation.

Coding agents tend to come in three shapes. Agents in your terminal or editor, working in your repository with your permissions. That's where most of the book's interactive work happens. Cloud agents, where you hand over a task, and a pull request comes back from a hosted sandbox. And kits for building agents of your own. Most vendors now offer all three.

Underneath, shared conventions are forming. An instruction file, like agents dot M D, that many tools can read. A common protocol, M C P, for connecting agents to tools and data. Skills, packaged know how that an agent loads only when it needs it. And hooks, small scripts that run the same way every time, around the agent's actions.

Models change fastest of all. Frontier commercial models still lead on long, multi file work. Open weight models have improved dramatically, and some run on a well equipped laptop. Many agent tools can point at a local model, so a laptop can drive a real agent loop. Bigger context windows haven't removed the need to curate context. And agentic work burns through tokens, so the cost advice in the book still applies.
So here are the questions to ask any tool. What can it see? What can it touch? How does it get feedback? How do you review its work? And what happens when it reads something hostile?

That last question isn't theoretical. Public incidents have shown agents with broad access leaking private data after reading a malicious issue or support ticket. The write ups are short and worth reading. And measure your results, because feeling fast and being fast are not the same thing.

Answer those five questions, and the product names stop mattering. The names on this page will change. The principles in the chapters will outlast every one of them. That's the whole crew, and the whole ship. Read the whole book, free, at the agentic crew dot com.
